Hook: In April 2019, Uber filed to sell its shares to the public. Its prospectus told investors how big its market was: 12.3 trillion dollars. 5.7 trillion for getting people around, 3.8 trillion for moving freight by truck, and 2.8 trillion for restaurant meals. Draw Uber's own revenue that year at the same scale. 10.4 billion dollars: less than a tenth of one percent of its market. By 2025 its revenue had grown five-fold, to 52 billion, and it was still under half of one percent. Was the twelve trillion wrong? Not exactly. It answered a different question from the one most people asked.

Four months later, the office company WeWork filed its own prospectus. It counted 255 million people in its target cities who might one day work at a desk, and multiplied by the 11,700 dollars a year that employers there spend on office space for each of them. Total opportunity: 3 trillion dollars. Six weeks later the share sale was withdrawn. In November 2023 the company filed for bankruptcy. Big markets are easy to write down. This part is about how to size one honestly: what to count, how to count it, and how to tell when a number is answering the wrong question.
Industry, Built. Part seven: sizing a market. How big is a market, and how would anyone know?
Guess: Chapter one. Run it: size a market.

Play it yourself. How much do Americans spend on bottled water in a year? You have six facts. There are about 337 million Americans. According to the Beverage Marketing Corporation, which tracks the industry, each drank about 46 gallons of bottled water in 2023. About seven tenths of it comes in single-serve bottles. A supermarket sells a pack of twenty-four half-litre bottles for, say, six dollars. A gallon jug costs, say, a dollar fifty. And the rest is jugs, home delivery, sparkling water and imports. Pause, and make your estimate. Write it down. Then we will see what three published sources say, and why they disagree with each other.

Here is one way to work it. Three hundred and thirty-seven million people times forty-six gallons is about 15.6 billion gallons a year. A pack of twenty-four half-litre bottles holds twelve litres, a little over three gallons, so at six dollars a pack that water costs about 1.89 a gallon. Seven tenths of the gallons at that price is about 21 billion dollars. The rest at a dollar fifty is about 7 billion more. Call it 28 billion dollars a year. If your number was anywhere near that, you did what a market analyst does: units times price. Now meet the published numbers.
Define: Chapter two. Definition is most of it.

Two published numbers for the same market, the same year. The Census Bureau, which surveys American businesses every year, says American bottled-water plants shipped 7.2 billion dollars of water in 2023. Primo Brands, which says it has the largest share of bottled water sold in American shops, told its shareholders the market was 25 billion dollars of retail sales. And your sum from the shelf was about twenty-eight. The second number is 3.5 times the first. Nobody made a mistake. They measured different things.

Every market size answers four questions, whether it says so or not. First, at which level of the chain? The Census counts what water is worth leaving the factory. By the time it reaches a shop till, a wholesaler, a truck and the shop itself have each added their share. Second, which plants? The Census files each plant under what it mainly makes. Water bottled in a plant that mostly makes soft drinks is counted with the soft drinks, not with the water. Third, which products? Still or sparkling, plain or flavoured, delivered in five-gallon jugs to offices, or imported from Fiji and France. And fourth, which buyers, which year, which money: homes or businesses, last year or this, dollars of the day or after inflation. Change any answer and the number moves, sometimes by billions. A market size without its definition is not a fact. It is half of one.
Top: The top-down way starts with what governments count. Every five years America takes an Economic Census, of every business with employees, and in between the Census Bureau surveys a sample of companies every year, asking what each of their plants shipped. Here is the answer since 2012: from 5.7 billion dollars to 7.5 billion in 2024, made by about 13,143 people. But some of that rise is only prices. Producer prices for bottled water rose by about a third between 2020 and 2023. Take out the price rises and the gold line is what was really shipped, at 2012 prices: much flatter. Top-down numbers are careful, consistent from year to year, and late. The concentration tables from the 2022 census, which Part 5 used, came out in April 2025. And they are only as good as the definitions behind them, which, as the last chapter showed, may not be the ones your question needs.

Chapter 2 said the census files each plant under what it mainly makes. Here is what that does. The census counts plants, not products. A brewery that also bottles some water is a brewery, and all of its water is counted as brewery shipments. A water plant that also makes some iced tea is a water plant, and its tea is counted as water. So an industry's total is the output of the plants filed under it, not the market for the product in its name. The two errors partly cancel, by an amount nobody can see in the totals. Every five years, the Economic Census also reports shipments product by product, which is closer to a market; in the years between, you have the plants.
Bottom: Chapter four. Bottom-up: units times price.

The bottom-up way builds a market out of units and prices, as you did with the shelf. The units are the easier half. Three hundred and thirty-seven million people at forty-six gallons each is about 15.6 billion gallons a year. The price is the hard half, because a gallon has a different price at every step of the chain. Divide the Census's dollars by those gallons and a gallon leaving the factory is worth about 46 cents. Divide Primo's retail figure by the same gallons and a gallon at the till is worth about 1.60. That is the gap between the two published numbers: roughly 3.5 times. Some of it is the truck and the shop. Some is water the Census files elsewhere, from soft-drink plants and from abroad. The bottom-up method makes you choose the price, and the price you choose decides which market you have measured.

The other bottom-up way is to add up the companies. The largest seller in American shops, Primo Brands, reported revenue of 5.2 billion dollars in 2024, at the prices it charges shops and offices, including home delivery, filters and coffee. But the other big sellers of bottled water are soft-drink companies, and their reports do not say how much of their revenue is water. Adding up companies works when they report the market you want, and that is rarer than it sounds. So the analyst ends up with a sum of the companies that do report, and a remainder that is a guess.
Homes: Chapter five. When adding up companies works.

Adding up companies can work very well, in one kind of market. Part 5 met the American home centers: 776 firms, of which the four largest made 98 percent of the sales. The 2022 census counted 258 billion dollars. Now add up just two companies' annual reports. Home Depot: 157 billion dollars. Lowe's: 97 billion. Together, 254 billion: within 1 or 2 percent of the census. Do not take the closeness too seriously. Home Depot alone took 61 percent of the census's total, Lowe's 38. And the two companies' revenue includes their stores in Canada and Mexico and some business that is not a home center, while the census includes Menards and smaller chains; the differences happen to roughly cancel. But the lesson stands: when a few companies hold almost the whole market, their own accounts are the best bottom-up estimate there is. When thousands of small firms share it, as nail salons do, adding up companies is hopeless, and only a census will do.

Now the opposite case, from the same census. Home centers: a few hundred firms, and two of them nearly the whole market. American nail salons: 33,066 firms, with sales of about 11 billion dollars in 2022. The four largest made 0.4 percent of those sales. Even the fifty largest together made only 2 percent. There are no annual reports to add up, and no company knows the market's size from its own books. So the method follows the market's structure, which is why Part 5's concentration tables come first. Few firms: add up their accounts. Many firms: count from the top, with a census, or from the bottom, with units and prices.
Three: Chapter six. Three answers, one market.

Put the three answers on one line. The Census, at the factory gate. Primo's figure, at the till. Your sum, from the gallons and the shelf prices, also at the till. Once each is put on the same definition, two of them agree to within a few billion dollars: American bottled water sold at retail for something like twenty-five to twenty-eight billion dollars in 2023. The Census figure is not wrong. It answers a different question: what American bottled-water plants were paid for what they made. That is triangulation. Put every estimate on the same definition before comparing them. When two methods agree, check that they do not secretly share an input: yours rests on the tracker's count of gallons, and Primo does not say where its number comes from. And report a range, with what its edges depend on, rather than one number with false precision.

The third rule deserves a picture. Go back to your own sum. It came to about 28 billion dollars, from four inputs. Now let each input be different, one at a time, across a range that seems fair. The pack price, from four fifty to eight dollars for twenty-four bottles, moves the answer from 23 to 35 billion. The share in single-serve bottles, the jug price and the gallons per person matter much less. Set every input at its edge at once and the range runs from about 19 to 39 billion. That is what a range is for: it tells you which number to go and check. Here, it is the price of a pack: the one number in your sum that you chose yourself.
Panels: Most market numbers you read come from firms that sell data, and each of them looks through one window. Scanner panels collect every barcode beeped at the tills of the shops that agree to share their data. They see supermarket bottled water in fine detail, and they miss vending machines, and the five-gallon jugs delivered to offices. Household panels ask families to record what they buy. People forget, and the families willing to do it are not quite like everyone else. Card and app data see what one bank's or one app's customers spend: never the cash, never the other banks. And surveys of companies, by statistical offices or trade bodies, are thorough and late, and file each plant by what it mainly makes. When two firms' estimates of the same market differ by a factor of two, the first question is not who is wrong. It is which window each of them was looking through.

And the windows move. In 2000, a panel built on the tills of shops saw nearly everything Americans bought at retail: less than 1 percent was sold online. Every year since, a larger share has gone where no till beeps. It jumped in 2020, when the shops closed, and it never fell back. By 2025, it was about 17 percent of all retail sales, about one dollar in six. A tracker that never moved its window would have seen many markets shrinking, when what had changed was where people bought. So when you read a market size, ask what its window was, and when the window was last moved.
Prices: A market measured in dollars is an area. Along the bottom, the number of units sold; up the side, the price of each. The dollars are the rectangle. Call it a hundred. Now let twice as many units be sold. And let the price halve. The rectangle changes shape completely, and its area, the market in dollars, is exactly where it started. So a market that is flat in dollars may be booming in units, or shrinking, and you cannot tell which from the dollars alone. To a first approximation, the growth in dollars is the growth in units plus the growth in price.

Both halves move, and in some markets they move fast. Here is what American consumers paid for computers since 2000, as the Bureau of Labor Statistics measures it. The statisticians adjust for quality: a laptop that is twice as fast for the same price counts as a price cut. Measured that way, the price fell by 92 percent. What cost a hundred dollars in 2000 costs about 8 now. New cars, measured the same way, rose by about a quarter, less than prices in general. So the same dollar figure means very different things in different markets. A computer market that is flat in dollars has grown enormously in what it delivers. Sizing a market is two forecasts, not one: how many, and at what price. The quantity is often the easier half, because people and their habits change slowly. The price is set by costs, competition and technology: everything Parts 4 to 6 were about.

Now split a real market this way. American bottled-water plants shipped 5.7 billion dollars of water in 2012, and 7.5 billion in 2024. Dollars up by 30 percent. The producer price index for bottled water rose by 20 percent over the same years, most of it in the burst of inflation after 2021; before that, the price had been falling. Divide the one by the other, and the quantity, the water itself, grew by only about 8 percent in twelve years. This is the gold line of Chapter 3, read as a rectangle: most of the market's growth in dollars was price. Whenever a company or a report tells you a market grew, ask the next question. Grew in what: in dollars of each year, in dollars of one year, or in things?
Tam: Go back to Uber's twelve trillion dollars, and read how it was built. Start with every passenger-car mile driven in 175 countries, seven and a half trillion of them, valued at what a mile of driving costs: 4.7 trillion dollars. Add every mile travelled on a bus or a train, four point four trillion of them, at about twenty-three cents a mile: another 1 trillion. So 'getting around' is worth 5.7 trillion. It includes every mile you drive in your own car to work, and every bus ride in a city where Uber does not operate. Uber's own trips in 2018 came to 26 billion miles. The prospectus said so itself: less than one percent.

The restaurant part was built the same way. The prospectus took a commercial tracker's estimate of everything the world's consumers spent in restaurants, cafés and bars in 2017, 2.8 trillion dollars, and split it by how the meal was eaten. Home delivery: 161 billion. Takeaway and drive-through: 634 billion more. Together, the 795 billion that Uber called the market it could serve. And then the TAM: all of it, the 2.0 trillion dollars of meals eaten at a restaurant table included, on the argument that some of those dinners might one day be delivered. Against that, Uber Eats took orders worth 7.9 billion dollars in 2018. Notice that this is what customers paid, food and all; Uber's own revenue was the cut it kept. And notice the years: a spend from 2017 set against orders from 2018. A good TAM reader checks both.

Prospectuses draw this as three rings. The outer one, the total addressable market: everything that could be done the company's way, if the whole world switched. Inside it, the serviceable market: the part where the company actually operates, and for the kind of trip it serves. For Uber, 2.5 trillion dollars. And at the centre, too small to see at this scale, what the company actually sells. Analysts sometimes add a third name for a ring between them, the serviceable obtainable market: the share the company could realistically win in the next few years. It is the one most worth arguing about, and the one prospectuses least often print. The outer ring answers a question about ambition: how big would this be if everyone did it our way? It is not a forecast, and it is not a market in the sense this series uses the word: buyers who are paying, now, for something, at a price. Read it as the company's dream, and look for the inner rings.

Now size the inner ring the other way, bottom-up, from the same prospectus. In late 2018 about 91 million people used Uber in a month. Over the year there were 5.2 billion trips, rides and meals together: about 57 for each of those people. They paid, on average, about 9.54 dollars a trip: 49.8 billion dollars in all, which Uber calls gross bookings. Most of that went to drivers and restaurants. Uber kept about a fifth: 10 billion dollars. People, times trips, times fare, times the share kept: that is a market you can check, line by line, against the company's own accounts. Twelve trillion dollars is not.
Bass: Chapter ten. How new things spread.

In 1969 a marketing professor, Frank Bass, wrote down why adoption traces an S. Picture a hundred households, and a new product. Each year, a few of the households that do not yet have it buy it on their own: they read about it, they like new things. Bass called that share p. Others buy it because their neighbours have it: the more neighbours, the more likely. Bass called that pull q. At first almost nobody has it, so there is nobody to copy, and growth is slow. Then copying takes over, and the curve goes steep. And at the end there is nobody left to convince, so it flattens. Two numbers, p and q, and a ceiling: that is the whole model. It even says when the rush comes. New adopters peak at the log of q over p, divided by p plus q, years after launch: here, about 6 years. The more people copy rather than choose on their own, the later and the sharper the peak.

Fit Bass's curve to real products and it does well, after the fact. The white dots are the share of American households with a microwave oven, year by year; the curve is the model, with its three numbers chosen to fit. The internet. Smartphones. Each fits closely, with a small p and a larger q: most people bought because others had. Here is the catch. These fits were made with the whole curve in hand, ceiling included. The question a market sizer faces is different: how high will the curve go, and how fast, when you can only see its first few years?
Early: Chapter eleven. Calling the curve early.

Put yourself in 1969. Colour television has been on sale for some years. These dots are all you can see: the share of American households with a colour set, rising to about a quarter. Fit Bass's curve to those years, and it says colour television is levelling off, at about 31 percent of homes: a luxury for a third of the country. Here is what happened. It kept climbing, to almost every home in America. The model was not wrong about the shape. It simply could not tell, from the bottom of the S, where the top would be. Nothing in the first quarter of a curve tells you whether you are looking at the start of a steep climb or most of a gentle one.

Why does it miss so badly? Look closely at what the first years contain. Here are colour television's four dots, up to 1969: none above a quarter of households. Now force the curve to stop at forty percent, and fit it. At sixty. At eighty. At a hundred. Every one of the four passes within about a third of a percentage point of every dot. The early years cannot tell these curves apart, because in the early years every S-curve looks the same: a slow start bending upward. The ceiling is simply not in the data yet. So a forecast of the ceiling has to come from somewhere else: from who could possibly buy, at what price, and from products that came before. The curve can tell you the shape. It cannot tell you the size.

Was colour television unlucky? Run the same test on every technology in the data with enough years to try it: 25 of them. For each, fit the curve to the years up to a quarter of households, and compare its forecast with the last year observed. About half land within ten percentage points. 8 miss by more than thirty, almost all of them on the low side: colour television, power steering, the refrigerator, the washing machine. The median miss is 12 points. So an honest forecast of a young market is a range, and a wide one, which is why careful forecasters publish scenarios and update them as the years come in. A single confident number for a market ten years out is a guess with decimals.
Replace: Chapter twelve. When everyone has one.

There is one more thing the S-curve hides, and it decides how big most markets are. Picture every microwave oven in American homes as water in a tub. Two taps fill it. Gold: homes buying their first one. Green: homes replacing one that wore out. And a drain at the bottom, the old ovens thrown away. Run the model from 1975, with the adoption curve of Chapter 10, the real count of American households, and an assumed life of ten years for each oven. In the early years nearly every sale is a first purchase. First purchases peak in 1983, at about 8 million a year. Then they fade, because almost every home has one. But the tub is now full, and full tubs drain: the ovens bought in the boom start to wear out, and replacements take over. By the 2020s, in this model, about 96 percent of the ovens sold each year replace an old one, and the rest go to households that did not exist before. The S-curve flattened; the market did not.

So a full market obeys a simple rule. Roughly, the number sold each year is the number in use, divided by how many years each one lasts, plus whatever the number of homes grows by. With about 127 million ovens in use, a ten-year life means about 13 million sold a year. If ovens lasted 8 years, 16 million. If they lasted 12, about 11 million. Two years of life, either way, moves the whole market by a fifth or more, with not one extra household. That is why, for anything most people already own, a car, a phone, a fridge, how long people keep it matters as much as how many people there are. The life is our assumption here; a real sizing would have to measure it, and the measuring is hard.
Register: Every number in this series has an entry like this one, in what we call the Register. A key, and the value. What exactly it measures, in words, because, as this part has shown, the definition is most of a number. Where it came from, and the address to check it. Two dates, and they are different: the period the figure describes, and the day we read it. Markets move; a figure read today about 2023 says so. And what kind of figure it is: a company's own filing, a statistical office, a commercial tracker's estimate, a study, a press report we could not check against its source, or this series' own assumption, labelled as one. Here, a note too: Primo does not say where its number comes from. Seven parts in, the Register holds 434 entries, and a check refuses to build a film that shows a number without one.

Here is what the Register holds, seven parts in. More than half of its 434 entries come from companies' own filings: 246 of them, read from annual reports and prospectuses lodged with regulators. Then 92 from statistical offices and regulators. Then studies, commercial trackers and press reports, each labelled as such, and 7 assumptions of our own. Before each part is built, every number it shows is read again from its source, and the dates are kept. An entry about 2017 read in 2026 is not wrong; it is history, and the film says so. That is the whole discipline: never a number without a source, a definition and a date.
Called: Every part ends with forecasts. This part's are market sizes that someone built on. WeWork's 3 trillion dollars counted every office worker in its target cities as a possible member. The share sale was withdrawn within weeks, and in November 2023 the company filed for bankruptcy. The opportunity was real in the sense that the money is spent on offices. It was never WeWork's to take. And a forecast still open: the Beverage Marketing Corporation expects Americans to drink about 50 gallons of bottled water each by around the end of this decade. In 2024 they drank 47.3. At the pace of the last year it would arrive on time; at the pace of the year before, it would not. A market size is only as good as its definition, and as the business that is built on it.

And this series' own call. When the Census Bureau publishes its figure for 2026, American bottled-water plants will have shipped more than seven and a half billion dollars' worth, against 7.46 billion in 2024. For it: Americans drink a little more bottled water every year, and the plants that make it are counted the same way each time. Against it: producer prices have been flat since 2023, and this series fell by a sixth in a single year, from 2022 to 2023. We put it at sixty-five percent, and will score it when the figure appears, in about the middle of 2028.

Every part of this series has made a call like that, with a date and a rule for scoring it. Here they are, ordered by when they come due. The first, on smartphone shipments, can be scored in 2027, when the year's first full count of phones shipped is published; the last, on jobs in health care, not until 2031. When a call comes due, the series will show the result in the part it belongs to, right or wrong, and keep the record. A forecaster who never writes down a number, a date and a probability can never be shown to be wrong, and so can never be shown to be any good.
